title: Run distributed inference with llama.cpp on Arm-based AWS Graviton4 instances (Aryan Bhusari, Joe Stech; Arm Learning Paths, last updated 09 Sep 2026; page is a 5-step tutorial: Introduction, Convert, Configure workers, Configure master, Next steps)
id_read: learn.arm.com/learning-paths/servers-and-cloud-computing/distributed-inference-with-llama-cpp/ (landing page) and sub-pages how-to-1, how-to-2, how-to-3, fetched as raw HTML and stripped; the catalog URL is truncated at 'distributed-inference-wit'
setup: 3x AWS c8g.4xlarge (Graviton4, 1 master + 2 RPC workers; page does not state vCPU/RAM, but the log shows 'RPC[...] - 31491 MiB free' per worker), model Llama-3.1-70B Q4_0 GGUF (37.22 GiB, 4.53 BPW, 80 layers, dense, not MoE), build 6209 (fb22dd07), workers started with 'rpc-server -c -p 50052 -H 0.0.0.0 -t 64', master 'llama-cli -n 128 --rpc $worker_ips -ngl 999'. Network type/bandwidth: not stated (only 'TCP connections between nodes'). Storage: 500 GB EBS (prerequisite). Batch 1, 10-token prompt, 63 generated tokens.

numbers.what: Generation speed in the page's example log
numbers.value: eval time 36101.93 ms / 63 runs = 573.05 ms/token = 1.75 tok/s
489542.78 ms (about 8.2 min); page says inference run 'will take ~10 minutes'
not stated anywhere on the 4 pages
numbers.where: all pages (grep for Gbps, bandwidth, 10G: nothing)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: guides report 2-5 tok/s for 70B on CPU clusters
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: this page's own log shows 1.75 tok/s (below the 2-5 range); the first pass said 'no tok/s on the page', which is also wrong: the number is on the 'Configure the master node' sub-page, not on the landing page

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 10GbE as the minimum
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: no network figure on any page of this learning path; the 10GbE claim must come from other guides

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: tensors held in worker RAM over the network (rpc-server holds weights in remote RAM)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 'RPC offloads both the model and the computation over TCP'; master physically hosts the GGUF and ships tensors to workers (-ngl 999); '-c' enables a local file cache on workers

why: Dense 70B layer sharding over RPC, not an expert store. All weights are resident in the workers' RAM; nothing is streamed per token; only activations cross the wire. Our regime fetches 10 of 512 experts per layer per token from NVMe into a 8/16/32 GB RAM cache, which is the opposite traffic pattern. The one useful datum is that stock llama.cpp RPC on three 16-vCPU Graviton4 boxes reaches only 1.75 tok/s for a 37 GiB dense model.
quality_loss: none discussed (Q4_0 quantisation only; no benchmark)
limitations: Tutorial; authors state RPC is insecure by default and supports at most 16 backend workers; the page text flags an 'AI-assisted summary'. No measurement methodology (single run, 63 tokens).
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction. pubtech F.md line 28 cites 'RPC guides report 2 to 5 tok/s with 10GbE as minimum'; this specific guide gives 1.75 tok/s and no link figure, so it cannot be the source of that sentence.

title: MegaScale-Infer: Serving Mixture-of-Experts at Scale with Disaggregated Expert Parallelism (Ruidong Zhu, Ziheng Jiang, Chao Jin, Peng Wu, Cesar A. Stuardo, Dongyang Wang, Xinlei Zhang, Huaping Zhou, Haoran Wei, Yang Cheng, Jianzhe Xiao, Xinyi Zhang, Lingjun Liu, Haibin Lin, Li-Wen Chang, Jianxi Ye, Xiao Yu, Xuanzhe Liu, Xin Jin, Xin Liu; ByteDance Seed + Peking University; arXiv v4 26 Jul 2025, cs.DC)
setup: Models (Table 4, bf16 weights/activations/KV): Mixtral-8x22B (56 layers, 8 experts, top-2, 141B), DBRX (40 layers, 16 experts, top-4, 132B), Scaled-MoE (48 layers, 32 experts, top-4, 317B). Cluster 1: 8 nodes x 8 NVIDIA 80 GB Ampere GPUs, 128 CPUs, 2 TB host RAM, 8x200 Gbps InfiniBand, 400 GB/s NVLink. Cluster 2 (heterogeneous): H20 nodes (900 GB/s NVLink, 4x400 Gbps NICs) + L40S nodes (PCIe, 2x400 Gbps). Workload: production trace, median input 571 / output 159 tokens, TBT limit 150 ms. Baselines vLLM and TensorRT-LLM (min 8 GPUs for Mixtral/DBRX, multi-node for Scaled-MoE). Decode throughput per GPU is the metric; batches are large (aggregated across many attention replicas; roofline discussion uses batch 156 per expert for an A100).

numbers.what: Decode throughput per GPU, Scaled-MoE, homogeneous Ampere
numbers.value: MegaScale-Infer 1.90x vs TensorRT-LLM and 7.11x vs vLLM (absolute tok/s only in Fig 8a bars, not in text)

numbers.what: Abstract headline 'up to 1.90x higher per-GPU throughput'
numbers.ratio: 1.90x (the figure is the best case, not the mean)

numbers.value: 1.86x per-cost decode (Intro), 1.80x per unit power decode / 1.72x e2e per unit power

numbers.what: Ablation: optimised M2N lib + ping-pong on top
Ablation: ping-pong micro-batches m=1 to 2 / m=3

numbers.value: median latency -80.8%, P99 -96.2%, throughput up to 9.9x (256 KB: -68.2% median, -92.9% tail, 4.2x)
cost of serving same traffic 1.5-2.0x lower (heterogeneous), ~10,000 GPUs

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Experts on separate GPUs over RDMA in datacentres
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: attention and FFN/expert modules are disaggregated onto different node groups (attention replicas with DP, experts with EP), tokens shipped M-to-N over RDMA (own M2N library on RDMA write-with-immediate); 200-400 Gbps NICs

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: up to 1.90x per-GPU throughput
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 1.90x is vs TensorRT-LLM on Scaled-MoE decode; vs vLLM it is 7.11x; end-to-end only 1.18x

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: hardware unverified / not on abstract page
catalog_numbers_correct.correct: wrong in the sense it is now known
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 8-GPU Ampere 80 GB nodes with 200 Gbps IB, plus H20/L40S heterogeneous cluster

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: 'disaggregates attention and FFN, not experts per se'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: abstract: 'disaggregates attention and FFN modules within each model layer'

why: Datacentre GPUs, bf16, decode batches aggregated into the hundreds per expert so FFN becomes compute-bound; the whole point is to raise batch per expert. Our regime is batch 1 where each expert sees one token, nothing to aggregate, CPU-only, experts on NVMe not on remote GPUs. Per-layer cross-node communication also adds latency (paper: TBT only 'comparable' to baselines). The one portable idea (separate the memory-bound expert store from attention) is the conceptual cousin of an expert store on another host, but the paper itself needs batch to make it pay.
ablation: Yes (Sec 7.4): disaggregation alone 4.66x over colocated; M2N library 1.53x more; ping-pong m=1->2 1.9x. All at large batch on GPUs.
limitations: Authors note communication overhead per layer, instability at high percentiles with NCCL, need for micro-batches >=3 for comm overlap; expert-load imbalance handled with on-device redundancy (Sec 8). No limitation section about small batch.
contradicts_our_findings: No. pubtech F.md calls it a datacentre GPU/RDMA system not comparable; confirmed from raw text.

title: Delta Decompression for MoE-based LLMs Compression (D2-MoE; Hao Gu*, Wei Li*, Lujun Li*, Qiyuan Zhu, Mark Lee, Shengjie Sun, Wei Xue, Yike Guo; HKUST / Univ. of Birmingham / AISpeech; arXiv v1 24 Feb 2025, cs.LG)
id_read: arXiv:2502.17298v1 (PDF, full text). The text carries no venue statement ('ICML 2025' comes from the catalog; the only ICML mention in the PDF is a reference).
setup: Models: Mixtral-8x7B (8 experts), DeepSeekMoE-16B-Base (fine-grained + shared expert), Phi-3.5-MoE (16 experts), Qwen2-57B-A14B. Experiments on NVIDIA A100 GPUs (count not given). Method (training-free): Fisher-weighted merge of all experts of a layer into one shared base weight W_b, deltas W_i - W_b compressed by truncation-aware SVD, semi-dynamic structured pruning of the base. Compression 20/40/60% (80% max). Calibration data and tasks: WikiText-2, PTB, C4 PPL; 7 zero-shot tasks (OpenbookQA, ARC-e/c, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, PIQA, MathQA). Baselines NAEE, MoE-I2, MC-SMoE, MoE-Compress, SparseGPT 2:4, ASVD, LoSparse. Speed test: Mixtral-8x7B, batch size 64.

numbers.ratio: accuracy 0.90x of original; PPL 1.33x original; vs NAEE +9 points (+19% rel.), vs MoE-I2 +8 points (+16%)

numbers.what: Qwen3-30B-A3B at ~50% (independent, from the LorExperts paper)

numbers.value: CKA between expert weights 0.3-0.5 (Fig 1); delta V matrices CKA ~0.9, U ~0.3 (Fig 5, App A.6)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Shared base plus per-expert delta, deltas compressed by SVD
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Fisher-merged base per layer + truncation-aware SVD of deltas + base pruning

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: 40-60% compression with quality loss
base is within a layer (merged experts)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: base merges all experts of one MoE layer; no cross-layer sharing

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: (ICML 2025)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: not stated in the arXiv v1 text; keep as catalog's claim, unverified from the paper

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: over 13% better than other compressors at 40-60%
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: abstract wording; consistent with +16-19% rel. accuracy at 40% on Mixtral

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: Qwen3-30B-A3B PPL 23.58 vs 8.50
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: this number is not in the D2-MoE paper; it is in LorExperts Table 4 (D2-MoE re-run by AMD)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: hardware not stated
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: A100 GPUs are stated; count not

why: Base is a merge of the experts in the same layer, so compressed deltas still need the base resident in RAM; there is no cross-layer or prediction-based residual. At 128-512 experts per layer a single Fisher-merge base is far from most experts (LorExperts shows D2-MoE degrading sharply on Qwen3-30B: PPL 23.58 vs 8.50). Quality loss is large at the ratios that would matter (40-60% bytes). Throughput table is GPU batch 64 and compares only to other compressors.
quality_loss: Table 2/3: Mixtral-8x7B avg zero-shot 0.63 -> 0.60 / 0.57 / 0.52 at 20/40/60%; WikiText-2 PPL 3.98 -> 4.65 / 5.28 / 6.46; Phi-3.5 40%: 0.62 -> 0.60; Qwen2-57B 40%: 0.59 -> 0.58. No MMLU/generative benchmark. Training-free, no fine-tuning.
ablation: Yes: Tables 5-9: merge method for base (Fisher PPL 5.28 vs frequency 6.42 vs TIES 12.45 on WikiText-2); base/delta compressors (Table 6: truncation-aware SVD 5.28 vs vanilla SVD 6.22); calibration data (Table 9); App A.6 shared-V / merged-U extreme compression (80% ratio PPL 12.95). None isolate cache or layout.
limitations: Impact-statement only; paper does not discuss limitations of expert count. Compression time reported (Table 10; delta SVD ~25 min on Mixtral).
contradicts_our_findings: Partly consistent. Their CKA 0.3-0.5 between experts (a function-space statistic, rotation invariant) is not a cosine; our median |cos| ~0.005 between Qwen3 experts and the LorExperts r<=0.21 co-activation/weight correlation agree that raw weights are near-orthogonal. D2-MoE's success on Mixtral (8 experts) is the regime where a single base works; its failure on Qwen3-30B (128 experts) is consistent with our 'no shared structure' result.

title: DeRS: Towards Extremely Efficient Upcycled Mixture-of-Experts Models (Yongqi Huang*, Peng Ye*, Chenyu Huang, Jianjian Cao, Lin Zhang, Baopu Li, Gang Yu, Tao Chen; Fudan / CUHK / Shanghai AI Lab / Baidu USA / StepFun; arXiv v1 3 Mar 2025, cs.LG, venue not stated in the text)
setup: Upcycled MoE only (experts initialised as copies of one dense FFN). Three tasks, six architectures: MoE-LLaVA (StableLM-2-1.6B, Qwen-1.8B, Phi-2-2.7B; 4 experts, top-2, every other block) on general multimodal benchmarks; Med-MoE (StableLM-2-1.6B, Phi-2-2.7B) on VQA-RAD/SLAKE/PathVQA; Coder-MoE (DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B) on HumanEval/MBPP. Training on 8x or 4x A100-80G (Tab S19). DeRS compression: expert = shared base + delta; delta sparsified (drop rate up to 0.99) or quantised (16 to 1 bit); DeRS upcycling: train sparse-matrix or low-rank deltas against a trainable shared FFN.

numbers.what: MoE layer parameters, DeRS compression, general multimodal

numbers.value: sparsification 0.99 drop rate or 1-bit deltas still without significant degradation
model size -52.7%, training memory -21.2%, inference memory -43.8%, overall performance +0.7%

numbers.what: Cosine similarity of trained experts to initial FFN and to each other

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Base plus sparse or quantized delta
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: DeRS-Sparsification / DeRS-Quantization (compression) and sparse-matrix / low-rank (upcycling)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: works for upcycled MoE where experts start as copies of one dense FFN, not for from-scratch MoE
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Appendix: 'not applicable to compressing MoE models trained from scratch ... impossible to extract redundant delta weights' since random init

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: up to 65% fewer parameters per layer without drop
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: abstract/intro wording

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 52.7% is the DeRS-LM upcycling (training-time) size cut, not the post-hoc compression figure

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: 2-bit deltas OK
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Sec 4.1; even 1-bit shown without significant drop on the 3 general models

why: Redundancy exists only because experts are fine-tuned copies of one FFN (cosine > 0.999). Real from-scratch MoEs (Qwen3-30B, our 125B-class 512-expert model) have near-orthogonal experts, and the authors state the compression is not applicable. Models are 1.3-2.7B with 4 experts and the evaluated metrics are VQA/code; no throughput or storage-I/O claims.
quality_loss: Reported as no significant drop on VQA/SQA/POPE etc. for upcycled MoE-LLaVA at 65%; differences in Table 1 are +0.2 to +0.3% for upcycling; no perplexity numbers. Fine-tuning data is the same as for vanilla upcycling (training required for upcycling variant).
ablation: Yes (Sec 4.4): freezing the shared base costs 1.3% / 1.6% (SM/LM); sparse rate and rank sweeps (Table 4); rank 64 degrades.
limitations: Authors state it needs a shared pre-trained initialisation; from-scratch training with DeRS upcycling may be capacity-limited (App D).
contradicts_our_findings: No; it supports the reading that cross-expert redundancy needs shared initialisation, which our Qwen3 probe lacks.

title: Breaking the MoE LLM Trilemma: Dynamic Expert Clustering with Structured Compression (Peijun Zhu, Ning Yang, Baoliang Tian, Jiayu Wei, Weihao Zhang, Haijun Zhang, Pin Lv; Guangzhou Univ., CASIA, Tianjin Univ., USTB; arXiv v4 21 Jul 2026, cs.CL; ICML 2026 submission template)
setup: Trained-from-scratch 12-layer Transformer, d_model=768, E=32 experts, G=8 groups, rank r=16, T=100 recluster interval, alpha=0.7, top-g1=1 group then top-2 experts; trained on 2 A100 GPUs with AdamW; evaluated on GLUE dev and WikiText-103 (plus pretraining Table 7 and long-text Table 8, not examined). Baselines Dense 110M, Switch-Top2 (875M), Expert-Choice, MoE-Lite (295M), D2-MoE (620M). Memory 'peak GPU memory (GB)'. Shared base FP16 + INT4 residuals; inactive groups offloaded to NVMe with EMA prefetch predictor (lookahead L=2 steps). The text never says whether a group spans experts of a single layer or a cross-layer set; compression formula is per group K*d_in*d_out -> d_in*d_out + K*r*(d_in+d_out).

title: Shape Mutating Expert Compression: LorExperts and BTExperts (Inesh Chakrabarti*, Sourjya Roy*, Bowen Bao, Thiago Crepaldi, Spandan Tiwari, Ashish Sirasao; Advanced Micro Devices; arXiv v1 7 Aug 2026, cs.LG)
id_read: arXiv:2608.07814v1 (PDF, full text; the catalog URL was an alphaxiv .md mirror)
setup: Models: Qwen3-30B-A3B (E=128, top-8; uncompressed PPL 8.50 on Wikitext-103, MMLU 77.8), Gemma-4-26B-A4B (uncompressed PPL ~7.15), Mixtral-8x7B for the gate_proj speedup arithmetic. ~50% expert compression: cluster experts per layer (k-medoids by co-activation NPMI or weight Frobenius distance), keep one full-precision dominant per cluster, store other members as neuron-permutation-aligned (Jonker-Volgenant) rank-r (r=64) residuals. Calibration: C4, 64 sequences x 2048 tokens. Eval: Wikitext-103 PPL plus LM-Eval-Harness MMLU/ARC-C/HellaSwag/WinoGrande/PIQA. Hardware: not stated. Baselines: M-SMoE, HC-SMoE, Freq-Prune, REAP, D2-MoE.

why: Supports our measurement that expert weights are near-orthogonal (within layer, here), and quantifies what a rank-64 + aligned-dominant scheme costs on the same Qwen3-30B-A3B we probed: ~50% fewer expert parameters at PPL +3.7 and MMLU -23.7. That is a lossy 2x byte cut with a quality price our lossless-byte plan avoids. It is within-layer and post-hoc, so it does not touch the cross-layer predicted-residual idea. Assumptions that break: GPU/HBM speedup argument (not NVMe), calibration needs activation data, quality loss not recoverable without more rank, and a dominant per cluster still needs to be read in full.
quality_loss: Qwen3-30B-A3B: PPL 8.50 -> 12.20, MMLU 77.8 -> 54.1, ARC-C 52.6 -> 37.1, HellaSwag 59.6 -> 52.6, WinoG 71.0 -> 68.4, PIQA 79.4 -> 75.3 (Coact-NPMI, ~50%). Gemma-4: PPL ~7.15 -> 14.66, MMLU 51.1 (uncompressed MMLU not in the extracted table row). Sweep Fig 5: accuracy drops mainly near 50%.
ablation: Yes (Appendix A, Table 6): tree (BTExperts) vs flat per-cluster decomposition (sharing corrections across a hierarchy does not beat flat on near-orthogonal experts); clustering metrics WS-Frob / Coact-NPMI / Msoft; protecting top-8 firing experts raises Qwen3 MMLU 42.4 -> 53.7. No ablation of alignment alone found in the extracted text.
limitations: Authors: calibration cost (per-member SVD + reconstruction fine-tuning ~500 steps), inference amortisation bounded and routing-dependent, closed-form Hessian-weighted fit is ongoing work; utilisation measured on WikiText-2 only, domain shifts change busy sets. Hardware not stated.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction; strengthens it. Caution for our probe: LorExperts aligns neuron permutations before forming residuals ('experts may be similar only up to a neuron permutation'); our raw element-wise cosine and residual test on Qwen3-30B (no permutation alignment, gate matrices only, 16 rows) does not test that. Their reported outcome with alignment (rank-64 keeps 26% energy, PPL +43%) is still far from lossless, so it would not rescue a ~1.0x byte bound, but the alignment case is untested by us.

title: Improving Parameter Utilization by Sharing Neural Experts Across Layers in Transformers (CS-MoE; Dian Jiao*, Jiaxin Duan*, Shuai Zhao, Jiabing Leng, Yiran Zhang, Feng Huang; China Electronics Cloud Technology Co.; arXiv v1 31 Aug 2026, cs.LG)
setup: Pilot (App. B): 'pre-trained Qwen3-MoE-4B' with 36 layers, 4 experts/layer, top-1; held-out validation 50,000 tokens from DCLM; linear CKA computed on Gram matrices of expert activations (not on weights); greedy zero-shot swap: each expert in deep layers 24-32 replaced by the shallow-layer (1-8) expert with highest CKA (>0.85 as 'redundancy indicator'), no fine-tuning, compared with random swaps at expert sharing ratio ESR 5% and 20%. CS-MoE proper: trained from scratch, 0.6B-12B (Qwen3 style), Megatron-LM on 8x NVIDIA H200 (up to 32 nodes for a 4.5T-token run); each layer has independent experts plus a global shared pool (M=324 for d=4096), per-token routing.

numbers.what: Base PPL of the pilot model
numbers.value: not stated in text (Fig 1 y-axis 10-80; authors call < 15 'acceptable')

numbers.what: Decode latency at batch size 1, 8x H200, 8B scale
numbers.value: Dense 14.2 ms/tok; standard sparse MoE 16.5; CS-MoE default 15.8; CS-MoE with cache optimisation 14.9
'45% reduction in unique memory traffic per token' (adjacent layers re-use shared experts in L2/SRAM)

numbers.what: Adjacent-layer overlap of top-10% shared experts
numbers.value: 68.4% (layer l vs l+1) falling to 42.1% (l vs l+5); Gini 0.28

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: Cross-layer sharing found by CKA above 0.85 on Qwen3-MoE-4B
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the 0.85 threshold and the 4-expert 36-layer model are in App B.1; it is a post-hoc zero-shot swap test on a pretrained model, not a training-time design (the training-time design is CS-MoE itself, which is trained from scratch)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: a training-time design
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the CKA finding motivates the training-time CS-MoE architecture, but the numbers in the pilot are zero-shot swaps

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: CKA is rotation-invariant so it does not imply element-wise similarity
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: App B.1 itself says CKA 'is invariant to orthogonal transformations' and chooses it to avoid permutation invariance of weights; moreover it is computed on activations, not weights
Table 4

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: 55% active params of dense at lower PPL

why: Two separable pieces. (1) The CKA swap evidence is functional (activation-based), 4 experts per layer, 36 layers, +1.2 PPL at 5% swapped: it says deep experts can sometimes be replaced by shallow ones, not that one is a byte-level residual of the other. For our 512-expert model it is unmeasured. (2) CS-MoE is a from-scratch architecture (retraining required) whose point is that the same expert is reused by multiple layers, so a cache of a shared pool would hit across layers; the only latency datum is a GPU batch-1 decode table (14.9 vs 16.5 ms/tok) with weights resident in HBM. Does not apply to already-trained 125B weights.
quality_loss: Pilot: PPL increase +1.22 to +3.98 for targeted swaps, base PPL not given. CS-MoE: PPL lower than dense at 55% active params; downstream Table 1/2 accuracy also reported (not itemised here).
ablation: Yes (Table 3): removing independent experts PPL 10.32 vs 10.08; pool size, top-K, load-balance coefficient alpha=0.01. No ablation of the cache effect separate from architecture.
limitations: Authors: validated only up to 12B; no tailored distributed infrastructure for a cross-layer pool; effects under RLHF/DPO/PEFT unknown. Pilot model and its pretraining are not described.
contradicts_our_findings: Not a contradiction of the cosine ~0 result (CKA on activations vs raw weights), but it is the first read paper showing functional cross-layer interchangeability on a pretrained MoE; our element-wise residual test cannot detect that, and our result must be worded as 'no byte-level cross-layer residual', not 'no cross-layer redundancy'. Worth knowing the pretrained 'Qwen3-MoE-4B' with 4 experts is not a public model I can verify.

title: DIMoE-Adapters: Dynamic Expert Evolution for Continual Learning in Vision-Language Models (Mengxin Qin, Xiang Zhang, Xi Wang, Kun Wei, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng; Xidian University; arXiv v1 8 May 2026, cs.CV)
id_read: arXiv:2605.07494v1 (PDF, full text; Figure 6 is an image, only its caption and text are readable)
setup: Continual-learning (MTIL) on CLIP ViT-B/16: each expert is a LoRA module, router is a single-layer MLP with Top-p gating (p0=0.6), experts grown/pruned by SCEE during training; single NVIDIA A6000. Appendix E: for each incremental task one randomly selected newly introduced expert is taken as the task representative; cosine similarity of expert parameter vectors is computed after training between experts of different tasks, shown as per-layer matrices (Fig 6, MTIL Order I).

numbers.what: Off-diagonal cosine similarity of task-specific LoRA experts
numbers.value: 'close to zero' across all (selected) MoE layers; no numeric value in the text

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: cosine similarity between expert parameter vectors across MoE layers is near zero
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the matrices are per layer, between experts of different TASKS (one random expert per task), not between experts of different layers; the experts are LoRA adapters on CLIP ViT-B/16, not pretrained LLM expert FFNs

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: so no cross-layer redundancy
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the paper makes no cross-layer claim; the conclusion drawn is that task-specific experts are 'nearly orthogonal rather than redundant'

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first-pass: wrong object (task adapters, not pretrained LLM expert weights)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: confirmed; additionally it is within-layer across tasks, not cross-layer

why: LoRA experts trained on different tasks from a shared init, in a CLIP vision encoder; near-zero cosine there is expected (independently trained low-rank updates in a high-dimensional space) and says nothing about pretrained LLM expert FFNs or about layer-to-layer similarity.
quality_loss: not applicable (analysis of a continual-learning method)
limitations: Qualitative figure only; one random expert per task is sampled.
contradicts_our_findings: No. But pubtech F.md (family 19 'Published methods vs measured') cites DIMoE-Adapters as literature for 'near-zero cross-layer cosine'; that citation should be dropped. The real supporting literature is LorExperts Table 1/Sec 2.2 (within-layer weight cosine vs co-activation r<=0.21; 'near-orthogonal') and Meta Expert App A.2 ('naive cosine similarities collapse toward zero' in high dimensions).
